highlights: The Diet extended its session to 28 August to debate the draft constitution, focusing on popular sovereignty, the Emperor's status, and the renunciation of war.
A severe staple food crisis forced SCAP to release 174,708 metric tons of imported cereals and canned goods to 20 deficit prefectures; Tokyo's average daily intake was only 1,352 calories.
At the IMTFE, eyewitnesses including Dr. Robert Wilson and Miner Searle Bates gave harrowing testimony on the 1937 Rape of Nanking, and General Myron C. Cramer replaced Justice Higgins.
Screening under the 4 January Purge Directive was substantially completed, barring prominent figures including Mitsu Kono and Haruo Matsui from public office.
Rival black-market gangs fought gun battles with police in Tokyo's Shibuya and Shimbashi districts, leaving six dead and prompting police to shut open-air stalls.
The Board of Communications was elevated to the Ministry of Communications on 1 July with Sadakichi Hitotsumatsu as minister, and mail rates rose 200 percent.

The first American raw cotton, 30,000 bales, reached Japanese mills for export yarn production, while coal shortages concentrated steelmaking at Yawata and held chemical output to 32 percent of minimum needs.
SCAP ordered 65 suspected war criminals apprehended, and 524,005 Japanese were repatriated during the month.

sections.summary: July 1946 overview: Diet debate on the draft constitution, purge screening substantially completed, critical food shortages with emergency releases to 20 prefectures, cholera in Fukuyama and Yokosuka, and new Citizens' Public Halls.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: SCAP General Orders No. 30 of 26 July discontinued the Office of Civilian Personnel as a special staff section; USAFPAC assumed its functions.
sections.title: Organization under SCAP

sections.summary: The Diet debated the draft constitution, focusing on popular sovereignty and the Emperor. Screening under the Purge Directive was substantially completed, and the Social Democrats rejected communist collaboration.
sections.title: Political Activities

sections.summary: Finance Minister Ishibashi outlined a recovery program stressing coal and fertilizer. Staple food shortages forced emergency releases of imported foodstuffs to 20 prefectures, and note circulation expanded rapidly.
sections.title: Economic Activities

sections.summary: Public assistance aided 2.19 million people; cholera struck Fukuyama and Yokosuka. The Ministry of Education set up Citizens' Public Halls and banned deleted wartime textbooks from 1 August.
sections.title: Social Activities

sections.summary: Diet extension to 28 August, purge of figures like Mitsu Kono, Communications ministry creation, Shibuya and Shimbashi black-market gang clashes, 65 war-crimes arrests, and IMTFE testimony on Nanking.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: The Diet extended its session to 28 August to consider the draft constitution and Ishibashi's economic policies. Purge screening removed figures like Mitsu Kono, and the Board of Communications became a ministry.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Rival black-market gangs fought gun battles in Shibuya and Shimbashi, prompting police to close open-air stalls. Tokyo crime nearly doubled since January; a fire destroyed 400 houses in Iida.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: SCAP ordered 65 suspected war criminals apprehended. The IMTFE heard testimony on Chang Tso-lin's 1928 assassination and the Rape of Nanking; General Myron C. Cramer replaced Justice Higgins.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: July economic developments: improved crop forecasts, coal at 1.66 million tons, steelmaking concentrated at Yawata, first 30,000 bales of American cotton, a 174,708-ton food release, and note circulation of 47.23 billion yen.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: Crop forecasts indicated improved 1946 harvests despite poor wheat and barley. June fish landings fell with the end of Hokkaido's herring season; 263 converted fishing vessels operated by late July.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Coal output reached 1.66 million metric tons in June, yet shortages hampered metallurgy and chemicals. Seventeen of 25 tracked minerals rose in May; Imperial Oil struggled with high costs.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: To conserve coal, iron and steel production was concentrated at Yawata. June chemical output met only 32 percent of minimum needs; 12 steel ships were completed.
sections.title: Heavy Industries

sections.summary: Machine tool output fell as makers feared reparations, but truck chassis rose to 1,483 units in June. Watch and clock production expanded to 62,193 units.
sections.title: Manufacturing

sections.summary: The first American raw cotton, 30,000 bales, arrived for export yarn production. Raw silk output dipped on coal and food shortages, while rayon pulp output tripled.
sections.title: Textile Industries

sections.summary: Rail freight fell to 8.14 million tons in June, and coal shortages left 72.5 percent of gas manufacturing capacity idle. The Nagamatsu hydroelectric plant was completed.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: The Board of Communications became a ministry on 1 July, and mail rates rose 200 percent. Vacuum tubes remained critically short; long-distance telephone service for Occupation Forces expanded.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: The Labor Disputes Adjustment Bill went to the Diet amid union protests. Government workers won a 50 percent wage increase; SCAP set a 40-hour week and paid leave for Occupation-employed laborers.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: In July 50 ships delivered 326,000 tons of imports, chiefly food, cotton, and phosphate. Exports included coal to Hong Kong and Korea, and raw silk and metals to the United States.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: SCAP released 174,708 tons of imported cereals and canned foods to 20 prefectures during a staple food crisis. Vegetable deliveries to urban legal markets plummeted after subsidies ended.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note circulation reached 47.23 billion yen by 20 July through deficit financing. SCAP permitted dissolution of the Yokohama Specie Bank and reviewed proposed national tax revisions.
sections.title: Finance

sections.summary: SCAP approved articles for the Holding Company Liquidation Commission, restricted further concerns including Titan Industrial, and revised the interim reparations list, deleting 60 plants and adding 21.
sections.title: Property Control and Reparations

sections.summary: July social developments: cholera controlled in Hiroshima and Kanagawa, Tokyo diets averaging 1,352 calories, 524,005 repatriates, Citizens' Public Halls, new geography textbooks, and journalism canons adopted by publishers.
sections.title: Part IV: Social

sections.summary: Cholera in Hiroshima and Kanagawa Prefectures was controlled and typhus fell sharply. Surveys found Tokyo's average daily intake only 1,352 calories; 524,005 Japanese were repatriated.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: The Ministry of Education started Citizens' Public Halls, reinstated geography with new textbooks, and screened teachers in Chiba. The Japan Newspaper Publishers and Editors Association adopted democratic canons of journalism.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

summary: Summation No. 10 covers non-military activities in Japan during July 1946, a critical transitional month marked by severe food shortages and historic institutional reforms. The report documents the acute food crisis that forced SCAP to release over 174,000 metric tons of imported cereals and canned goods across 20 deficit prefectures to prevent widespread starvation. In the Diet, intense debates centered on the draft constitution, particularly the concepts of popular sovereignty, the symbolic status of the Emperor, and the renunciation of war. Concurrently, the government substantially completed the purge of militarists from public office and established the Ministry of Communications. In the economic realm, coal shortages severely curtailed industrial output, prompting the concentration of all steelmaking at Yawata, while the arrival of the first 30,000 bales of American raw cotton began revitalizing the export textile sector. At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, prosecution witnesses provided harrowing eyewitness testimony regarding the Mukden Incident and the Rape of Nanking. For historians, this issue provides invaluable empirical data on May nutrition surveys, black-market gang warfare in Tokyo, labor union reorganization, and early Occupation governance.
